title: Blocking: A Reader Stuck Behind an Uncommitted Writer
description: A reader blocks behind an uncommitted writer's exclusive lock; row-versioning (RCSI) lets it read the last committed version without waiting. Why it matters: blocking is one of the most common production incidents in any transactional system -- and one of the hardest to reproduce in testing, since it only bites under real concurrent load.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine a single-occupant bathroom in an office. If someone walks in and locks the door, everyone else who needs it has to stand outside and wait, no matter how urgent their business is. SQL Server locking works the same way, and "blocking" is what happens when one person waiting behind that locked door is just a paying customer who wanted to peek in and check something quickly, not even use the room themselves.

In everyday terms: this lesson is about what happens when two pieces of work touch the same row of data at the same time — one of them is changing it, the other just wants to look at it. Most people assume that "just reading" is harmless and should never have to wait. In SQL Server's default configuration, that assumption is wrong, and this lesson is about why.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Any database that lets many users work on the same data at once needs a way to stop them from stepping on each other's toes. If two people could freely read and write the same row simultaneously with zero coordination, you'd get corrupted results — someone reading half-updated data, or two updates clobbering each other. The traditional fix, used by SQL Server's default isolation level (called READ COMMITTED, in its classic locking form) is: before you touch a row, you have to get a "lock" on it, like a key to that bathroom door. There are different flavors of lock. A reader takes what's called a **shared (S) lock** — think of it as "I'm looking, but so can anyone else who's just looking." A writer takes an **exclusive (X) lock** — "I'm changing this, nobody else touches it until I'm done, not even to look." Shared locks get along fine with other shared locks (many people can peek into the room together, so to speak), but an exclusive lock is incompatible with everything, including another shared lock. That incompatibility is the entire mechanism behind blocking.

**How it actually happens, mechanically, inside SQL Server.** Picture two sessions, A and B. Session A starts a transaction — a transaction is just "a block of one or more statements that either all happen or none happen" — and it updates a row, say deducting money from Alice's bank balance. The instant that `UPDATE` runs, SQL Server grants session A an exclusive lock on that specific row. Crucially, SQL Server does not release that lock the moment the statement finishes executing. It holds the lock until the entire transaction ends, whether that's a `COMMIT` (keep the changes) or a `ROLLBACK` (undo them). If session A's application code does something slow after the `UPDATE` — call a web service, wait on user input, run an unrelated report — that lock just sits there the whole time, held hostage by whatever the app is doing.

Now session B comes along and tries to run a plain `SELECT` on that same row, just to display Alice's current balance on a screen. To do that safely, B's `SELECT` needs to take a shared lock. SQL Server checks: is there an incompatible lock already sitting on this row? Yes — A's exclusive lock. So B's request is put on a wait list. This is what "blocking" means: session B is not doing anything wrong, it is not stuck in a loop, it has simply asked to enter a locked room and has to wait outside until the person inside comes out. B will sit there, frozen, potentially for as long as A's transaction takes to finish — which could be milliseconds, or if A's app is badly behaved, could be seconds or worse.

**Why this matters in production.** This single mechanism — readers waiting behind writers — is one of the most common sources of "the app suddenly got slow" incidents in real systems. It rarely shows up in development, because a developer testing alone never has two things colliding on the same row at the same time. It only bites under real concurrent load, with many users hitting the same popular rows (a shared inventory count, a popular customer record, a hot queue table) at the same moment. When it happens, the symptom looks confusing: the query itself is fast and simple, the "slowness" isn't really about the query at all — it's about waiting for someone else's lock to be released. If you look at SQL Server's live activity through system views like `sys.dm_exec_requests`, a blocked session shows up with a `blocking_session_id` pointing at whoever is holding the lock, and a wait type like `LCK_M_S` (waiting for a shared lock). Recognizing that pattern — a fast query that's mysteriously "hanging" with a wait type instead of a CPU-heavy execution plan — is a core diagnostic skill for anyone doing performance work on a real production database.

The lesson that follows walks through exactly this scenario happening live, and then shows the two ways out: either make the writer's transaction shorter so it doesn't hold the lock as long, or change how readers behave entirely by turning on row versioning (a feature called RCSI, short for READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT — a setting that lets a reader see the last version of the row that was committed, instead of demanding a lock and waiting for the current writer to finish).

**Try it yourself.** In the interactive scenario below, you control both sessions directly and can watch this entire chain of events happen in slow motion — Session A takes its exclusive lock, Session B goes into a blocked state waiting on it, and only once A commits does B's `SELECT` finally return. Pay attention to the timeline: the delay B experiences has nothing to do with how complex its `SELECT` is (it's about as simple as a query gets) — it's purely a function of how long A's transaction stays open. That single observation is the whole diagnostic skill this lesson is building: when a simple query is slow, don't assume the query itself is the problem before checking whether it's actually just waiting behind someone else's uncommitted work.

## Scenario
Session A updates Alice's account inside a transaction and then does other work before committing. Session B just wants to **read** the same row — and hangs until A commits.

## Why it's slow
Under the default `READ COMMITTED` isolation (locking version), A's `UPDATE` takes an **exclusive (X) lock** on the row and holds it for the whole transaction. B's `SELECT` needs a **shared (S) lock**, which is incompatible with X, so B **blocks** in a lock-wait chain until A releases. The longer A's transaction runs, the longer everyone behind it waits.

## What to look for
- In the timeline: A **acquires** an X lock; B goes **blocked** waiting on that lock; B only proceeds after A commits.
- On a real server: `sys.dm_exec_requests` shows B with `blocking_session_id = A` and a `LCK_M_S` wait.

## The concept
Writers block readers only because readers take shared locks. Turning on **READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI)** makes readers use **row versioning** — B reads the last committed version from the version store and never waits. The complementary fix is operational: keep write transactions short so locks are held briefly.

hints: B is waiting for a lock A holds. Which lock types are incompatible here (X vs S)?
Either stop readers from taking shared locks, or make A's transaction shorter.
Enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so readers use row versioning and don't block.

interleaving.description: Session A holds an uncommitted UPDATE; Session B's SELECT blocks behind it.

A.sql: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE AccountId = 1;

B.sql: SELECT AccountId, Owner, Balance FROM Accounts WHERE AccountId = 1;

interleaving.solutionNote: Enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (row versioning) so B's SELECT reads the last committed version without waiting; and/or shorten A's transaction so the X lock is released promptly.
